evidence.text: If group B streptococcus infection is identified in the woman, trans man or non- binary person within 72 hours after the baby's birth: • ask those directly involved in the baby's care (for example, a parent, carer, or healthcare professional) whether they have any concerns in relation to the clinical indicators listed in box 2 and • identify any other risk factors present and • look for clinical indicators of infection. Use this assessment to decide on clinical management (see recommendation 1.10.3 for the framework for making antibiotic decisions). [2021] Box 2: Clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection (observations and events in the baby), including 'red flags' Red flag clinical indicators: • apnoea (temporary stopping of breathing) • seizures • need for cardiopulmonary resuscitation • need for mechanical ventilation • signs of shock Other clinical indicators: • altered behaviour or responsiveness • altered muscle tone (for example, floppiness) • feeding difficulties (for example, feed refusal) • feed intolerance, including vomiting, excessive gastric aspirates and abdominal distension • abnormal heart rate (bradycardia or tachycardia) • signs of respiratory distress (including grunting, recession, tachypnoea) • hypoxia (for example, central cyanosis or reduced oxygen saturation level) • persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborns • jaundice within 24 hours of birth • signs of neonatal encephalopathy • temperature abnormality (lower than 36°C or higher than 38°C) unexplained by environmental factors • unexplained excessive bleeding, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal coagulation • altered glucose homeostasis (hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia) • metabolic acidosis (base deficit of 10 mmol/litre or greater)

Refer to NICE's guidelines on fever in under 5s and suspected sepsis in under 16s when assessing babies for late-onset neonatal infection who have been admitted to the hospital from home. [2021] Be aware that some pulse oximeters can underestimate or overestimate oxygen saturation levels, especially if the saturation level is borderline. Overestimation has been reported in people with dark skin. See also the NHS England Patient Safety Alert on the risk of harm from inappropriate placement of pulse oximeter probes. Table 2: Clinical indicators of possible late-onset neonatal infection (observations and events in the baby) Category Indicators Behaviour Parent or care-giver concern for change in behaviour Appears ill to a healthcare professional Does not wake, or if roused does not stay awake Weak high-pitched or continuous cry Respiratory Raised respiratory rate: 60 breaths per minute or more Grunting Apnoea Oxygen saturation of less than 90% in air or increased oxygen requirement over baseline Circulation and hydration Persistent tachycardia: heart rate 160 beats per minute or more Persistent bradycardia: heart rate less than 100 beats per minute Skin Mottled or ashen appearance Cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue Non-blanching rash of skin Other Temperature 38°C or more unexplained by environmental factors Temperature less than 36°C unexplained by environmental factors Alterations in feeding pattern Abdominal distension Seizures Bulging fontanelle This table has been adapted from the high-risk criteria in table 1 of NICE's guideline on suspected sepsis in under 16s.

Box 2: Clinical indicators of possible early-onset neonatal infection (observations and events in the baby), including 'red flags' Red flag clinical indicators: • apnoea (temporary stopping of breathing) • seizures • need for cardiopulmonary resuscitation • need for mechanical ventilation • signs of shock Other clinical indicators: • altered behaviour or responsiveness • altered muscle tone (for example, floppiness) • feeding difficulties (for example, feed refusal) • feed intolerance, including vomiting, excessive gastric aspirates and abdominal distension • abnormal heart rate (bradycardia or tachycardia) • signs of respiratory distress (including grunting, recession, tachypnoea) • hypoxia (for example, central cyanosis or reduced oxygen saturation level) • persistent pulmonary hypertension of newborns • jaundice within 24 hours of birth • signs of neonatal encephalopathy • temperature abnormality (lower than 36°C or higher than 38°C) unexplained by environmental factors • unexplained excessive bleeding, thrombocytopenia, or abnormal coagulation

Use the following framework, based on the risk factors in box 1 and the clinical indicators in box 2, to make antibiotic management decisions as directed: • In babies with any red flag, or with 2 or more 'non-red-flag' risk factors or clinical indicators: － follow the recommendations in the section on investigations before starting antibiotics and － start antibiotic treatment according to the recommendations in this guideline and － do not wait for the test results before starting antibiotics • in babies without red flags and only 1 risk factor or 1 clinical indicator, use clinical judgement to decide: － whether it is safe to withhold antibiotics and － whether the baby's vital signs and clinical condition need to be monitored. If monitoring is needed, continue for at least 12 hours using a newborn early warning system • for babies without risk factors or clinical indicators of possible infection, continue routine postnatal care as covered in NICE's guideline on postnatal care. [2021]

calls.role: You are the evidence synthesis agent.

claims.text: The patient's respiratory rate of 74 breaths per minute at 12 hours of age meets the threshold for raised respiratory rate (60 breaths per minute or more) and constitutes a clinical indicator of possible early-onset neonatal infection.

The oxygen saturation of 90% at 12 hours of age is consistent with the clinical indicator of hypoxia, defined as reduced oxygen saturation level, which is a non-red-flag indicator of possible early-onset neonatal infection.

Serial observations show a trend of respiratory deterioration, with respiratory rate increasing from 48 to 60 to 74 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation decreasing from 98% to 94% to 90% over the first 12 hours of life.

Given the presence of two or more non-red-flag clinical indicators (raised respiratory rate and hypoxia), the guideline framework directs to follow recommendations for investigations before starting antibiotics and to start antibiotic treatment without waiting for test results.

If clinical judgement is used to withhold antibiotics in a scenario with fewer indicators, monitoring must continue for at least 12 hours using a newborn early warning system; however, the current presentation of multiple indicators triggers the antibiotic initiation pathway rather than the monitoring-only pathway.

Clinicians should remain vigilant for red flag clinical indicators such as apnoea, need for cardiopulmonary resuscitation, need for mechanical ventilation, or signs of shock, which would further confirm the severity of the condition and necessitate immediate intervention.

calls.role: You are an independent source-entailment auditor. Check citation scope, exact evidence support, negation, contradictions and source applicability.

reasons: C1 cites E2 (Table 2) which explicitly defines clinical indicators for 'late-onset neonatal infection', whereas the patient is 12 hours old (early-onset window 0-72h) and the claim asserts the indicator is for 'early-onset neonatal infection'. While E3 supports tachypnoea as an early-onset indicator, the specific threshold of '60 breaths per minute or more' is only explicitly defined in the late-onset table (E2). Applying a late-onset specific threshold to an early-onset patient without an explicit early-onset threshold in the provided evidence is a population mismatch/unsupported inference.

calls.role: You are an independent neonatal safety auditor. Check patient age/gestation, trends, renal impairment, allergy, danger signs, missing data, and unsafe reassurance or discontinuation. Guidance is not an automatic treatment order.

C4 is supported: E4 states that for babies with '2 or more non-red-flag risk factors or clinical indicators', clinicians should start antibiotics and not wait for test results. The patient has at least two indicators (tachypnoea/RR 74 and hypoxia/SpO2 90).
C5 is supported: E4 correctly describes the monitoring pathway for babies with only 1 risk factor/indicator, distinguishing it from the current patient's status.
C6 is supported: E3 lists apnoea, CPR, mechanical ventilation, and shock as red flag indicators for early-onset infection.
